title: How Few-Shot Examples Add Up: A Causal Decomposition of Function Vectors in In-Context Learning
claim: A combined result emerges from additive parts, reweighted by attention and refined geometrically toward the true target direction.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed dividers, vector arrows and attention-mechanism blocks
description: Three panels separated by dashed vertical lines, each titled in bold serif. (a) Linear Superposition: three rounded boxes (Ex1 Ambig, Ex2 Unambig, Ex3 Ambig) with arrows v1, v2, v3. Ex2 is teal and the others are gray. Below, the vectors are chained head to tail on axes and compared with a dashed 'Overall FV' line. (b) Attention Reweighting Mechanism: a dark blue 'Query Last Token' box sends a thick teal 'High QK Match' arrow to the teal Key/Value Ex 2 column. Thin gray arrows go to the other columns, which hold Key/Value boxes for Ex 1, Ex 3 and x_{n+1}. A funnel icon sits below with the formula FV_ctx ≈ α1·v1 + α2·v2 + α3·v3. (c) Geometric Vector Refinement: a 2-D Dim1/Dim2 plot with a gray naive-sum vector, a blue refined vector, a dashed red true-task direction, and a red curved arrow labeled 'Shifted by Attention'. Teal marks the emphasized item throughout, and gray marks the others.
caption: Overview of FV formation in in-context learning. (a) Linear superposition: the \(n\)-shot function vector (FV) is approximated as a weighted sum of example-level sub-FVs. (b) Attention reweighting: contextualization modulates attention over demonstrations, changing the weights assigned to different sub-FVs. (c) Geometric refinement: contextualization further improves FV quality by altering the FV direction via pathway-specific updates, most consistently through Query--Key routing.
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) excels at new tasks from minimal examples, yet we still lack a mechanistic explanation of how few-shot prompts shape a model's function vector (FV)--a causal activation direction that drives task behavior on the ICL query. Across tasks and models, an $n$-shot FV is well-approximated by a linear combination of example-level sub-FVs, suggesting additive and composable contributions from individual demonstrations. Beyond additivity, we show that models contextualize individual examples' representations based on prior examples to adaptively reweight which demonstrations dominate the FV: attention shifts toward examples that are more informative and less ambiguous under the context. Finally, a causal decomposition separates Query-Key routing from Value updates, finding that contextualization's most consistent contributions to FV quality arise from Query-Key alignment--particularly in ambiguous settings--while Value-mediated effects are more heterogeneous. Together, these results unify additive superposition with context-dependent attention reweighting into a mechanistic, testable account of how few-shot prompts implement tasks.
